summary.heading: Systems, signs and the first law
summary.html:
• Closed system: no mass in or out, but energy can transfer by heating or work. Isolated system: neither mass nor energy.
  • Clausius sign convention: $Q$ = net thermal energy supplied to the system (negative if it loses energy); $W$ = net work done by the system (positive when expanding, negative when compressed).
$$Q = \Delta U + W$$
  • The first law is conservation of energy for a closed system.

summary.heading: Work done and change in internal energy
summary.html:
$$W = P\Delta V \qquad \Delta U = \frac{3}{2}nR\Delta T = \frac{3}{2}Nk_B\Delta T$$
  • $W = P\Delta V$ only at constant pressure (from $F = PA$ moving a distance $\Delta x$). When the pressure changes, $W$ = area under the p–V graph.
  • For an ideal monatomic gas, $\Delta U$ depends only on $\Delta T$. Also $\Delta U = \frac{3}{2}\Delta(PV)$, handy when given pressures and volumes.

summary.heading: Four types of process
summary.html:
ProcessFixedFirst law becomes
isovolumetric$V$$W = 0$, $Q = \Delta U$
isobaric$P$$Q = \Delta U + P\Delta V$
isothermal$T$$\Delta U = 0$, $Q = W$
adiabaticno heat flow$Q = 0$, $\Delta U = -W$
  • Isothermal: slow, in good thermal contact; all heat supplied becomes work.
  • Adiabatic: insulated or very fast. Expanding, the gas does work from its own internal energy and cools; compressed, it heats up.
$$PV^{\frac{5}{3}} = \text{constant}$$
  • For adiabatic changes of an ideal monatomic gas. An adiabat is steeper than an isotherm through the same point.

summary.heading: Cycles, heat engines and the Carnot cycle
summary.html:
• A heat engine runs a cycle that returns the gas to its start, so $\Delta U = 0$ per cycle (net $Q$ = net $W$). It takes in $Q_h$ from a hot reservoir, does work $W$, and gives out $Q_c$ to a cold reservoir: $W = Q_h - Q_c$.
$$\eta = \frac{\text{useful work}}{\text{energy input}} = \frac{W}{Q_h} \qquad \eta_{\text{Carnot}} = 1 - \frac{T_c}{T_h}$$
  • Net work per cycle = area enclosed by the loop. Clockwise: an engine. Anticlockwise: net work is done on the gas (fridge, heat pump).
  • Carnot cycle: isothermal expansion at $T_h$ (takes in $Q_h$), adiabatic expansion (cools to $T_c$), isothermal compression at $T_c$ (gives out $Q_c$), adiabatic compression (back to $T_h$).
  • No engine between two reservoirs can beat the Carnot efficiency. Temperatures in kelvin; 100% would need $T_c = 0$ K.

summary.heading: The second law of thermodynamics
summary.html:
• Kelvin form: no cyclic engine can take thermal energy from a hot reservoir and turn it all into work; some must go to a cold reservoir.
  • Clausius form: thermal energy cannot flow spontaneously from a colder body to a hotter one (a fridge needs work done on it).
  • Entropy form: the total entropy of an isolated system never decreases. Constant for a reversible process; increases for an irreversible one.
  • Real processes (friction, turbulence, heat flow across a temperature difference) are irreversible, so the entropy of a real isolated system, and of the universe, always increases.

summary.heading: Entropy
summary.html:
$$\Delta S = \frac{\Delta Q}{T} \qquad S = k_B\ln\Omega$$
  • Entropy measures the disorder of the particles: how spread out their energy and positions are. Unit $\text{J K}^{-1}$. Gas > liquid > solid; hotter and larger volumes have more.
  • $\Delta S = \dfrac{\Delta Q}{T}$ for energy transferred at constant $T$ (in K): positive for energy in, negative for energy out.
  • Macrostate: the overall description (5 heads from 10 coins). Microstate: one particular arrangement. All microstates are equally likely, and disordered macrostates have far more of them. $\Omega = 1$ gives $S = 0$.
  • Local decreases: a non-isolated system's entropy can fall (water freezing, living things growing) if the surroundings' entropy rises by at least as much.

summary.heading: Watch out for
summary.html:
• Sign errors: $W$ is negative for a compression; $Q$ is negative when the gas loses energy.
  • Saying no heat flows in an isothermal process ($Q = W$), or that the temperature is constant in an adiabatic one.
  • Using $W = P\Delta V$ when the pressure changes (use the area).
  • Forgetting $\Delta U = 0$ over a whole cycle.
  • Celsius in $\eta_{\text{Carnot}}$ or $\Delta S = \frac{\Delta Q}{T}$.
  • Efficiency as $\frac{W}{Q_c}$ or $\frac{Q_c}{Q_h}$ instead of $\frac{W}{Q_h}$.
  • Saying entropy can never decrease (it can, locally).
  • Calling $k_B$ the Stefan–Boltzmann constant.

Global impact: The steam engine came before the theory. Can students name another technology that worked long before anyone understood why?
Carnot's limit means every thermal power station wastes most of its fuel's energy. How does that shape the case for and against different energy sources?
Theories: Ask students to show that if the Clausius form were false, an engine could break the Kelvin form. Why does showing two statements are equivalent strengthen a theory?
The first law is about quantity of energy, the second about its direction. Why do we need both?
Shared endeavour: The founders of thermodynamics argued publicly about who had discovered what, and what the laws meant. Is fierce disagreement good or bad for science?
Carnot worked with the wrong (caloric) theory of heat, yet his conclusion that the maximum efficiency depends only on the two reservoir temperatures survived. How is that possible?
Models: Boltzmann's counting model links entropy to probability. Use the coin example: why does a "tidy" arrangement become so unlikely as the number of coins grows?
Boltzmann faced strong opposition from scientists who doubted atoms. What did his model assume that could not yet be tested?

oracy.html:
Opinion line (whole class, 8 minutes): students stand between "agree" and "disagree", explain their place, and may move after hearing others. Claim: "Leaving the fridge door open in a closed, well-insulated kitchen will cool the kitchen down."

  • I'm standing here because …
  • I moved after hearing …, because …
  • Where does the energy go when …?

Listen for: energy taken from inside the fridge is released by its coils into the same room, and the electrical work done on it ends up there too: the kitchen warms.

Can a law be based on probability?: Shuffle a new pack of cards: could it come back in order? Why do we treat "absurdly unlikely" as "impossible"?
Is a law that is certain in practice but not in principle weaker than one that is exact?
Why does time have a direction?: Play a short clip backwards (a glass breaking, milk mixing into coffee). How do students know it's reversed, and what physics do they use?
If the arrow of time comes from entropy, why do we remember the past and not the future?
Can we know the fate of the universe?: Heat death relies on treating the universe as an isolated system. How could we know whether that is true?
Compare a prediction we can never test with a claim about the distant past. Are both equally scientific?
Does technology drive science, or scienc: Find an example each way: steam engines led to thermodynamics; quantum theory led to lasers and transistors. Which direction is more common today?
Does it matter for knowledge whether a discovery came from curiosity or from a practical need?
